title: Records: transparent carriers for data
goal: By the end you can write a record whose compact constructor checks and tidies every instance, explain what javac generates for it, and say exactly where its equality and immutability stop.
opening:
Picture the front desk of a small town library. To borrow books, you fill in a loan slip: your member number, the titles, and the date they're due back. It sits in a clear sleeve, so anyone can read every box, and nothing is written on the back. Two slips filled in the same way stand for the same loan. Before a slip is stamped, the clerk at the counter checks it.

Programs are full of slips like that: small classes that only carry data. For years Java made you write them by hand: fields, a constructor, getters, `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`. That's five places that must agree on what the data is, and nothing makes them agree. Someone adds a box and updates three places out of five, and the program quietly treats two different slips as one.

The design patterns track was about objects that carry behavior. This track is about the data they carry. In this lesson, we'll let a record write those five places from one line, give it a counter where every instance is checked, and find where its promises stop. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: `record Masked(String phone)` overrides its accessor so that `phone()` returns `"****0123"` for the number 01614960123. What does `toString()` return?
options: `Masked[phone=****0123]`, because toString calls the accessor
`Masked[phone=01614960123]`
Nothing: it doesn't compile, because record accessors can't be overridden
`Masked@1b6d3586`, because overriding an accessor turns off the generated toString
warmup.why: The generated `toString`, `equals` and `hashCode` read the private field directly, not the accessor, so the full number reaches the log. Overriding an accessor is legal as long as the return type matches. To hide a component, override `toString` itself, as the lab does. The section on equality and immutability shows it with real output.

sections.h: A record is its components, and javac writes the rest

aside.title: Can a component have any name?
aside.body: Almost any. The Java Language Specification forbids eight: `clone`, `finalize`, `getClass`, `hashCode`, `notify`, `notifyAll`, `toString` and `wait`. Each one would give the record an accessor with the same name as a method of `Object`, so javac stops with `illegal record component name wait`. A plain Kotlin data class turns `val wait` into `getWait()`, so the clash doesn't come up there. In Java, a waiting time is `expectedWait`, which reads better anyway.

try.title: Look inside a record
steps: Run `RecordAnatomy` (or its Kotlin twin) with the command below. Predict the `==` line before you look.

From `labs/`, print the bytecode of the nested record: `javap -p -c 'modernjava/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/modernjava/l01/demo/RecordAnatomy$Shelfmark.class'`. Find the three `invokedynamic` lines.

Run `javap -v` on the same file and look for `BootstrapMethods`. Then run `javap -p modernjava/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/modernjava/l01/demo/Shelfmark.class` and compare what kotlinc generated.

code.title: RecordAnatomy.java

alt.title: RecordAnatomy.kt
alt.src:
package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo

// Naive: written by hand. The shelf was added later, and not to every method.
class OldShelfmark(val section: String, val shelf: Int) {               // shelf added later
    override fun equals(other: Any?) = other is OldShelfmark && other.section == section   // nobody updated this
    override fun hashCode() = section.hashCode()
    override fun toString() = "OldShelfmark(section=$section)"
}

// a plain data class: Kotlin generates equals, hashCode, toString, componentN and copy
data class Shelfmark(val section: String, val shelf: Int)

// the same data class, also emitted as a real JVM record (java.lang.Record subclass)
@JvmRecord
data class ShelfmarkRecord(val section: String, val shelf: Int)

/** What kotlinc gives a one-line data class, seen from the outside. */
fun main() {
    val old12 = OldShelfmark("FIC", 12)
    val old40 = OldShelfmark("FIC", 40)
    println("by hand:    $old12 equals $old40: ${old12 == old40}")

    val a = Shelfmark("FIC", 12)
    val b = Shelfmark("FIC", 12)

    println("toString:   $a")
    println("properties: section=${a.section} shelf=${a.shelf}")
    println("equals:     ${a == b}, same hashCode: ${a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()}")
    println("===:        ${a === b}   (two objects, each with its own identity)")
    println("isRecord:   ${Shelfmark::class.java.isRecord} for the data class, ${ShelfmarkRecord::class.java.isRecord} with @JvmRecord")
    println("components: ${ShelfmarkRecord::class.java.recordComponents.contentToString()}")
    println("superclass: ${ShelfmarkRecord::class.java.superclass.name}")
    println("copy:       ${a.copy(shelf = 13)}")

    synchronized(a) {   // compiles and runs: a data class instance is an ordinary identity object
        println("locked on a data class")
    }
}

try.expect: The first line shows the hand-written class calling two different shelves equal: `OldShelfmark[section=FIC] equals OldShelfmark[section=FIC]: true`. Then the record prints `Shelfmark[section=FIC, shelf=12]`, `equals: true`, `==: false`, `isRecord: true` and the components `[java.lang.String section, int shelf]`. The Kotlin twin prints `isRecord: false` for the plain data class and `true` for the `@JvmRecord` one. In the `javap -v` output, the bootstrap method is `ObjectMethods.bootstrap`, and its arguments include the string `section;shelf` and two `REF_getField` handles on the private fields. The Kotlin class has `getSection()`, `component1()`, `copy(java.lang.String, int)` and `copy$default(...)` instead.

The Kotlin twin prints `tampered stream gave: PageRangeK(first=5, last=1)` for the plain data class, an object its own `init` forbids, and rejects the `@JvmRecord` one. JDK 21 rejects it with `constructor is not canonical, so its first statement must invoke another constructor of class Shelfmark` and `call to this must be first statement in constructor`.

sections.h: Equality and immutability go one level deep
sections.body:
Start with what `equals` compares. Two records are equal when they're the same record class and every component is equal. For a reference component that means `Objects.equals`. For a primitive it means the wrapper's `compare` method returns 0, which holds two surprises for a `double`. A record holding `NaN`, the "not a number" value, equals another one holding `NaN`, though `NaN == NaN` is false. And records holding `0.0` and `-0.0` aren't equal, though `0.0 == -0.0` is true. Kotlin data classes behave the same way.

Arrays are worse. An `int[]` component compares by reference, so two records with equal arrays aren't equal, and `toString` prints something like `[I@1b6d3586`. Use a `List` instead.

A `List` component brings the real trap. Picture a form with a box that says "see attached list", and a list stapled behind it. The form is checked and stamped, but whoever kept a copy of the attached sheet can still write on it. A record holds a reference to whatever list the caller passed in. Here a crate of books is on its way to the North branch, and the program keeps the crates it sent in a set:

```java
// a crate of books on its way to a branch library
record Crate(String branch, List<String> titles) {}

var titles = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Dune", "Emma"));
var crate = new Crate("NORTH", titles);
var sent = new HashSet<>(Set.of(crate));
titles.add("Ulysses");             // someone reuses their list
sent.contains(crate);              // false: the hashCode changed under the set
```

```kotlin
// a crate of books on its way to a branch library
data class Crate(val branch: String, val titles: List<String>)

val titles = mutableListOf("Dune", "Emma")
val crate = Crate("NORTH", titles)
val sent = hashSetOf(crate)
titles += "Ulysses"                // someone reuses their list
crate in sent                      // false: the hashCode changed under the set
```

The `ShallowDemo` in the Try it prints:

```text
crate now:          Crate[branch=NORTH, titles=[Dune, Emma, Ulysses]]
hashCode changed:   true
sent.contains:      false
```

The crate is still in the set. The set just looks for it in the wrong place: a `HashSet` files each element under its `hashCode`, and that number changed after the crate was filed. Nothing threw. The fix is one line in the compact constructor:

```java
record SafeCrate(String branch, List<String> titles) {
    SafeCrate { titles = List.copyOf(titles); }          // an unmodifiable copy of the caller's list
}
```

```kotlin
data class SafeCrate(val branch: String, val titles: List<String>) {
    companion object {                                    // Kotlin can't reassign the parameter
        fun of(branch: String, titles: List<String>) = SafeCrate(branch, java.util.List.copyOf(titles))
    }
}
```

`List.copyOf` makes an unmodifiable copy, and it throws `NullPointerException` for a null element, which is what you want for library data. Kotlin's `List<String>` is a read-only view, not an immutable list: the caller may still hold the same object as a `MutableList`. So a data class needs the same copy, made in a factory. *Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal* in the concurrency track made this point about threads. Here the cost is a lost crate, even with one thread.

**A record is only as immutable as its components. Copy collections on the way in.**

The last trap looks like a fix. To keep a member's phone number out of the logs, someone overrides the accessor, so `phone()` returns `****0123`. The demo prints `accessor: ****0123` and then `toString: Masked[phone=01614960123]`. The generated `toString` reads the field directly (those were the getters in the bootstrap arguments), so the logs never ask the accessor. The override breaks a promise in the `Record` Javadoc too: a copy built from the accessors, `new Masked(m.phone())`, should equal `m`, and the demo prints `false`. To hide a component, override `toString` itself, as the lab does.

Every slip is now checked at the counter and safe from other people's pens. Which leaves a fair question: how do you change one?

alt.title: WitherDemo.kt

try.expect: Both versions print the original loan, the renewed one with 35 days and two titles, `same titles list object: true`, and a rejected `days must be positive: -1`. Withers and `copy()` both reuse the component references, which is safe here only because the list can't change. The blank-id check belongs in the compact constructor, so every wither gets it for free. In Kotlin, `first == first.copy()` is `true` and the copy's `note` is empty: body properties are ignored by `equals` and not copied.

compare.title: A checked shelfmark in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Shelfmark.java

kotlin.title: Shelfmark.kt

compare.note: Both give you `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` over all components, final fields, and a check that every construction goes through, including Kotlin's `copy()`. Three things differ. Java's compact constructor can tidy a parameter before it becomes a field; a data class can only reject it, so tidying lives in a factory and the public constructor stays open to raw input. Java deserialization rebuilds a record through its canonical constructor but skips a data class's `init` (`@JvmRecord` closes that gap). And Kotlin has `copy()` with named arguments, while Java has hand-written withers until JEP 468 ships, which it hasn't.

worked.title: Turn a hand-written membership form into a record

steps.say: When someone joins the library, the program fills in a membership form. Here it is as a JavaBean, a class with a getter and a setter for every field. It hands out its live list of branches, and its hand-written `equals` and `toString` weren't updated when the phone number was added. Any code can change a form after it was checked.

Write the header. The components are the whole state, and every setter is gone. Recompile: each place that called a setter is now a compile error, which is your list of code that changed a form after it was filled in.

steps.alt_code:

Add only the wither the library needs. Members do change their phone numbers, so `withPhone` earns its place. It calls the canonical constructor, so a changed form can't skip the checks. In Kotlin, `copy(phone = ...)` already exists and runs `init`.

drill.title: A checked member number from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `record MemberId(String value)` that rejects null, trims and upper-cases the value, and then rejects anything that isn't `M-` followed by four to six digits. Then write the Kotlin version. Which of the two can store the tidied value without a factory?

recap: A record is a final class whose header lists its components. javac writes private final fields, accessors, one canonical constructor, and `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` from that list, so they can't drift apart.

Check and tidy in the compact constructor. Every path goes through it: `new`, factories, other constructors, withers and Java deserialization. Kotlin's `init` is the twin, but it can't tidy a parameter, and Java deserialization skips it unless the class is `@JvmRecord`.
Equality compares every component: `Objects.equals` for references and `compare` for primitives, so `NaN` equals `NaN` and `0.0` doesn't equal `-0.0`. Arrays compare by reference.

Records are only shallowly immutable. Copy collection components with `List.copyOf`, or a changed list loses its record in a `HashSet`. The generated methods read fields, not accessors, so hide a secret in `toString`.
Kotlin generates `copy()`; Java has hand-written withers, because JEP 468 is on hold and in no JDK.
The limit: a record can't keep state beyond its components or hide its representation, and it's still an identity object. A class that needs a private cache goes back to writing everything by hand.
closing:
We started at the front desk, with a loan slip in a clear sleeve. A record is that slip: its components are the boxes, javac writes what we used to keep in five places, and the compact constructor is the counter every instance passes, whichever door it came through. Its promises stop one level down, at the attached list and the masked accessor.

Now look in your own code for a class with `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` written by hand. Compare the fields each one uses. If the three lists differ, you've found a drifting form.

Next, we'll fix which kinds of form exist at all. How can the compiler know it has seen every kind of library item?

quiz.q: `record Crate(String branch, List<String> titles)` is a key in a `HashMap<Crate, String>` that records where each crate is. The code that built the crate later calls `titles.add("Persuasion")` on its own list. What does `map.get(crate)` most likely return now?
options: The location, because records are immutable
`null`, because the key's hashCode changed and the map looks in the wrong bucket
It throws ConcurrentModificationException
The location, because HashMap compares record keys with ==
quiz.why: The record's fields are final, but the list they point to is the caller's list. `hashCode` includes the list, so it changes, and the map searches a bucket where the entry isn't. Nothing throws. Copying the list in the compact constructor prevents it.

quiz.q: Which of these makes `new Shelfmark("fic", 12)` equal to `new Shelfmark("FIC", 12)`?
options: `public Shelfmark { this.section = section.toUpperCase(); }`
`public String section() { return section.toUpperCase(); }`
`public Shelfmark { section = section.toUpperCase(); }`
`public Shelfmark(String section, int shelf) { section = section.toUpperCase(); }`
quiz.why: In the compact form you reassign the parameter and javac assigns the field afterwards. Assigning `this.section` there doesn't compile. The accessor override leaves the fields different, and `equals` compares fields. The full canonical constructor in the last option never assigns the fields, so it doesn't compile either.

quiz.q: A Kotlin `data class PageRange(val first: Int, val last: Int) : Serializable` checks `first <= last` in `init`. A program deserializes a tampered stream that says first = 5, last = 1. What happens?
options: You get `PageRange(first=5, last=1)`: Java deserialization doesn't run `init`
`InvalidObjectException`, because `init` runs during deserialization
`IllegalArgumentException` from `require`
`ClassCastException`, because the stream no longer matches the class
quiz.why: Java deserialization builds a plain serializable class without calling its constructor, so `init` never runs and the invalid object comes back. A Java record, or the same data class marked `@JvmRecord`, is rebuilt through its canonical constructor, and the stream is rejected with `InvalidObjectException`.

quiz.q: From the memory model track: `record OpeningHours(Map<String, String> days)` copies the map with `Map.copyOf` in its compact constructor. A new `OpeningHours` is published through a plain, non-volatile field. What is guaranteed for a thread that reads the new reference?
options: Nothing: without volatile it may see a null map
It may see a half-built map
Nothing, because records have no final fields
It sees the map as the constructor left it, because record fields are final, though it may keep reading the old reference for a while
quiz.why: Record fields are private final, so final-field rules apply: a thread that sees the reference sees the fields, and the map built in the constructor, as the constructor left them. A plain field doesn't promise when the new reference becomes visible. Publish it through a volatile field if readers must see updates promptly.

quiz.q: `data class Copy(val isbn: String) { var shelf = "FIC 12" }`. Copy `a` sits on shelf FIC 12. Copy `b` has the same ISBN and sits on REF 3. What is `a == b`?
options: `false`, because the shelves differ
`true`
It doesn't compile: data classes can't have body properties
It depends on which object was created first
quiz.why: Only primary-constructor properties take part in a data class's `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString` and `copy()`. `shelf` lives in the body, so Kotlin ignores it. A Java record can't have body state at all, so the question can't arise there.

flashcards.front: What does javac generate for `record Shelfmark(String section, int shelf)`?
flashcards.back: Private final fields, accessors `section()` and `shelf()`, a canonical constructor `Shelfmark(String, int)`, and `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`. The class is final and extends `java.lang.Record`.

flashcards.front: In a compact constructor, how do you tidy a component?
flashcards.back: Reassign the parameter: `section = section.trim();`. javac assigns the fields after the body. `this.section = ...` doesn't compile.

flashcards.front: A record overrides its accessor to mask a phone number. What does `toString` print?
flashcards.back: The full number. The generated `toString`, `equals` and `hashCode` read the fields, not the accessors. Override `toString` instead.

flashcards.front: `record R(double d)`: is `new R(Double.NaN).equals(new R(Double.NaN))` true?
flashcards.back: Yes. Primitive components compare with `Double.compare`, which treats NaN as equal to itself. And `0.0` doesn't equal `-0.0`.

flashcards.front: How do you make a record with a `List` component safe as a map key?
flashcards.back: Copy it in the compact constructor: `titles = List.copyOf(titles);`. The copy is unmodifiable and rejects null elements.

flashcards.front: Does Java deserialization run a Kotlin data class's `init` block?
flashcards.back: No, so a tampered stream can build an invalid object. A Java record, or a data class marked `@JvmRecord`, is rebuilt through its canonical constructor.

flashcards.front: Can you write `loan with { days = 35; }` in Java today?
flashcards.back: No. Derived record creation (JEP 468) is a Candidate JEP, on hold since at least January 2026, and in no JDK. Write withers by hand.

terms.plain: One of the values in a record's header, like one box on a form. Each one gets a private final field and a public accessor.
The constructor whose parameters match the components in order. Every other way of making the record goes through it.
The canonical constructor written without a parameter list. Its parameters are locals you can check and reassign; javac assigns the fields at the end.
The generated public method that returns a component. It's named after the component: `section()`, not `getSection()`.
The fields can't be reassigned, but the objects they point to may still change.
A method that returns a copy of a record with one component changed. Java has no generated ones.
A Kotlin annotation that compiles a data class to a real `java.lang.Record`.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate says: "Our `MemberCard(String phone, List<String> branches)` record is immutable, so it's safe to keep in a `HashSet` and to log as it is." Explain, in your own words, the two ways that can go wrong and what you would change.
explain_back.answer: A record is only shallowly immutable. Its fields can't be reassigned, but `branches` points to whatever list the caller passed in, and if the caller keeps changing that list, the record's `hashCode` changes and the set can't find it any more. I'd copy the list in the compact constructor with `List.copyOf`. Logging is the second problem: the generated `toString` prints every component, so the member's full phone number goes into the logs. Overriding the `phone()` accessor doesn't help, because `toString` reads the field directly. I'd override `toString` and print only the last four digits there, or better, make the phone a `PhoneNumber` record that masks itself.

sources.title: Brian Goetz, Data Classes and Sealed Types for Java (2019)
